title: Verifier‑Augmented versus LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The preregistered design employed gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes (from archived analysis artifacts) are exact and deterministic: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Diagnostics using execution and reconciliation artifacts show that shared_initial_generation together with reuse of the same deterministic validator created a deterministic ceiling that made the primary estimand uninformative in this run. We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results, an operational diagnosis of the ceiling mechanism supported by provider_call_audit and validator traces, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates feasibility of intent→configuration translation in prototypes and benchmarks; separate work shows verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The end‑to‑end operational safety question motivating this study is: under compact action‑aware staging semantics, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline?

We address this question with a fully preregistered paired binary design (N=400 pairs) executed under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The design intentionally used shared_initial_generation to isolate the verifier’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs and to conserve model calls. The primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline). All execution traces, validator traces, task manifests, and analysis outputs were archived and form the evidentiary basis for every numeric claim below.
sections.related_work: Three literatures frame the study and our recommendations. First, intent→configuration generation: recent demonstrations and datasets show LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates, but evaluations are typically on curated corpora or testbeds rather than production networks; representative examples include intent‑to‑configuration prototypes and pretrained/fine‑tuning efforts. Second, verifier‑guided workflows and deterministic verification: studies in IaC and provisioning (verifier‑guided training and verifier‑in‑the‑loop systems) and deterministic network verifiers document that strong verifiers catch many classes of errors offline, but closed‑loop runtime integration and joint generator×verifier dynamics remain underexplored. Third, agentic/tool‑augmented architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) broaden AIOps capabilities but introduce failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and overconfident outputs—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and evaluation‑gap reviews call for action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollout, repair, rollback, and provenance; our compact benchmark operationalizes these elements and reveals a concrete paired‑design pitfall when generation and scoring are deterministically coupled.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study preregistration (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1) specified a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 paired tasks and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The primary test was a permutation‑based paired difference test; exact McNemar and paired bootstrap CIs were prespecified for corroboration.

Execution contract and deterministic choices. We executed the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acting both as the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer. The preregistered generation_semantics used shared_initial_generation (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task a single LLM candidate was generated and routed identically to both baseline and guarded episodes. This choice reduced model calls (model_calls_used = 400 for 800 episodes; maximum_model_calls = 800) and isolated the validator’s acceptance decision on identical outputs. The adapter allowed up to one repair call in the guarded episode; repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, replay, and scoring. Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with per‑task difficulty metadata (level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were applied and passed for all pairs. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with full intent‑constraint validation (scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation", validator_version = "5.0"); validator traces record validation_before/after, final_configuration, repair_applied, and normalized_configuration. All measurements and analyses used archived artifacts without manual adjudication.

Statistical procedures and seeds. The preregistered confirmatory pipeline produced an exact paired contingency table; prespecified inferential outputs reported here are the permutation p‑value, exact McNemar two‑sided p, Cohen’s h, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and bootstrap_resamples = 10,000.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run began 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed = 800; failed = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation). Deterministic replay checks passed for every pair; no exclusions occurred.

Confirmatory, artifact‑grounded outcomes. The archived analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) reports: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen’s h = 0.0. These values are reproduced verbatim from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and analysis/*.csv).

Repair, rollback, and difficulty aggregation. Across 800 episodes repair_applied = 0 and no rollbacks were triggered; validator traces show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state in accepted configurations. The archived task manifest reports difficulty distribution (artifact extraction): medium: 80 tasks (20.0%); hard: 160 tasks (40.0%); very_hard: 160 tasks (40.0%).

Provider and reconciliation diagnostics. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact documents provider_call_audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 400, cache_miss_count = 400, stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 400}, condition_counts: {shared: 400}, cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, and all deterministic consistency checks passed. Validator traces for representative tasks show validation_before == validation_after and valid = true for every evaluated episode; repair_applied = false in every validator_trace entry. These artifacts jointly demonstrate that identical shared candidates were produced per pair and were deterministically accepted by the same validator implementation used for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling mechanism and construct validity. Two preregistered design choices produced a deterministic ceiling in this run. First, shared_initial_generation removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the identical deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When that deterministic validator accepts a shared candidate, both conditions necessarily record safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference is forced to zero. Provider_call_audit (stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 400}) and validator_trace fields (validation_before.normalized_configuration == validation_after.normalized_configuration and valid = true across examples) constitute artifact‑grounded evidence for this mechanism.

Statistical interpretation. The confirmatory tests (permutation, exact McNemar) and the bootstrap CI correctly reflect the observed data (p = 1.0, CI = [0.0,0.0). However, because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene on distinct generator outputs, these inferential results carry no information about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The original power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline failure rates; that assumption was falsified by the frozen generator+validator pairing, invalidating the prespecified sensitivity and power arguments for detecting a positive guard effect in this run.

Practical hardening recommendations (artifact‑grounded, implementable). To preserve opportunities for runtime guards to accept, block, or request repair, future preregistered designs should avoid conflating generator variance and scorer invariance. Specific, artifact‑grounded steps (each directly implementable using the archived manifests and traces) are: (1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition obtains a distinct LLM candidate; (2) Use a distinct post‑hoc scorer or held‑out adjudicator (different implementation or a validator with stochastic perturbation) to avoid conflating runtime blocking and measurement; (3) Controlled adversarial seeding to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates (select seeds/tasks from the archived manifest that the generator historically fails on absent verifier intervention); (4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling using task_manifest difficulty labels to ensure target representation of very_hard tasks; and (5) Instrumented mitigation metrics (repair_attempts, repairs_applied, time‑to‑rollback) recorded as explicit numeric outcomes. Each recommendation is supported by artifacts: task_manifest contains per‑task difficulty labels and expected_final_state; validator_traces contain repair_applied and validation timestamps; provider_call_audit documents generation semantics and model call accounting.

Operational implications. For operationally meaningful evaluation of runtime verifier utility, experimenters must: (a) create generation variance across conditions so guards can act; (b) separate runtime blocking logic from scoring logic to avoid tautological agreement; and (c) explicitly ensure the benchmark contains tasks that produce nontrivial baseline failure rates (controlled adversarial or targeted seeding). Without these elements a paired confirmatory estimand of guard utility is likely to be uninformative even when execution and scoring are deterministic and reproducible.

Threats to validity and limitations. Internal validity here is reduced by shared generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime and scoring. External validity is limited by the single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator. Construct validity is constrained because the validator does not model telemetry noise, asynchronous state, or stochastic adjudication. Adversarial robustness was not exercised in this run and remains open. The archived artifacts fully document these limitations so future registered runs can address them deterministically.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). The deterministic ceiling is a design artifact caused by identical per‑pair generation and reuse of a deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring; it renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here (independent generation per condition, distinct scorer, controlled adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification, and mitigation metrics) provide concrete steps to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings. Future runs that implement these hardening steps—possible using the archived task manifest and validator traces—can exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors meaningfully and restore inferential relevance for the primary estimand.

disclosure_statement: Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1. The immutable initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but none were applied (repair_applied = false). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle and were used without manual adjudication.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in the task manifest and can be aggregated by auditors; Table 1 reports the artifact‑extracted aggregated counts and percentages.
